To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the weight-averaged sedimentation coefficient of reversibly interacting systems with changes in fluorescence quantum yields is not equal to the population-weighted average, and that this is caused by the reaction-coupling of transport in the reaction boundaries of the interacting species.
the sedimentation velocity signal of reversibly associating macromolecular complexes is not necessarily the population-weighted average, if the signal changes with complexation.

the sedimentation coefficient of a rapidly reversible complex can be influenced by changes in the signal of the fluorophore, such that the signal-weighted average sedimentation coefficient can deviate significantly from the population-weighted average sedimented signal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel methods to study the structure, dynamics, and function of macromolecular assemblies.
the sedimentation of interacting macromolecules with changes in fluorescence quantum yields.
the development of a general binding model for sedimentation velocity analytical ultracentrifugation that can account for hydrodynamic cotranport in the presence signal changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the signal-weighted average sedimentation coefficient from sedimentation velocity analytical ultracen- tifugation with fluorescence is a useful tool for the study of reversible binding interactions of fluorescent macromolecules, but that its interpretation should be based on an explicit model that accounts for the observed signal changes.

sedimentation velocity analysis of reversibly interacting systems can be used to determine stoichiometries, binding affinities, and complex sizes, provided that all species have the same fluorescence quantum yield or the changes in fluorescence quantum yields are taken into account.

sedimentation coefficient distributions from transport methods are not necessarily population-weighted averages, but can contain contributions from reaction-coupled transport, which can be accounted for by effective particle theory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sedimentation coefficient of a reversibly interacting system with signal change is the signal-weighted population-weighted average, not the population-weighted average.
sedimentation coefficients are not always population-weighted averages, but can be signal-weighted averages in the case of systems with signal changes upon association.

the weight-average signal- and population-based sedimentation coefficients are equivalent only when the signal is constant with complex formation, and that the population-based average is not a general description of the transport method.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the weight-averaging assumption is not generally true for interacting systems with signal changes.
the weight-averaged sedimentation coefficient from transport methods is a population-weighted average, and that the population weights are not necessarily equal to the signal weights.

sedimentation velocity with fluorescence detection can be used for the determination of binding affinities and stoichiometries in systems with signal changes, provided that the reaction boundary is sufficiently thick and that the signal changes do not depend on the complex stoichiometry.
